query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified, single‐phase FeNiCrMn, the absence of Co intrinsically lowers the stacking fault energy such that deformation twinning becomes the dominant dynamic mechanism under high strain-rate and low temperature conditions. This twinning-mediated plasticity, operating in tandem with dislocation glide, enables the alloy to maintain its strength–ductility balance across regimes, while at higher temperatures or lower strain rates, dislocation glide with enhanced dynamic recovery predominates.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified and homogenized, single‐phase equiatomic FeNiCrMn with minimal secondary phases or precipitates.
generation.intervention: Perform dynamic mechanical tests (tensile or compressive) over a structured range of temperatures and strain rates to activate and distinguish between dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing performed under controlled atmospheres across a temperature range (e.g., 100 K, 300 K, and 500 K) and strain rates spanning from low (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) to high (≈10³ s⁻¹), with in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM and digital image correlation).
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and propagation of deformation twins that interact with and reinforce dislocation networks.
generation.mechanism: The Co-free composition lowers the stacking fault energy in FeNiCrMn, facilitating the formation of deformation twins at conditions where atomic mobility is limited (i.e., low temperature and high strain rate). These twins act as additional barriers to dislocation motion, enhancing work hardening and maintaining ductility. Conversely, at higher temperatures or lower strain rates, increased atomic mobility suppresses twinning and favors dislocation glide with dynamic recovery.
generation.predicted_outcome: A regime-dependent transition: at low temperatures/high strain rates, a twin-dominated deformation mechanism will be observable (evidenced by increased twin density, higher flow stress and enhanced work hardening) relative to a dislocation-glide dominated regime at elevated temperatures/low strain rates. This behavior contrasts with similar Co-containing alloys which do not exhibit a pronounced twinning effect under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Co-containing equiatomic alloys (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) which under similar testing conditions show predominantly dislocation-mediated plasticity with less pronounced work-hardening and lower twin density.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to well-homogenized, single-phase FeNiCrMn specimens. Deviations may occur with significant impurity levels, unintentional secondary phases, or processing-induced defect states that alter the effective stacking fault energy.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise stacking fault energy values in FeNiCrMn and their modulation with temperature and strain rate, as well as how subtle processing variations might affect the balance between twinning and dislocation glide.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare FeNiCrMn samples using controlled casting and homogenization. Subject samples to in situ mechanical testing at selected temperatures (e.g., 100 K, 300 K, 500 K) and across a wide range of strain rates (from ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ to ~10³ s⁻¹). Utilize in situ TEM and digital image correlation to capture the evolution of microstructural features such as twin boundaries and dislocation patterns during deformation.
measurements: Stress-strain curves (yield stress, flow stress, work hardening rates)
In situ TEM observations quantifying twin density and dislocation structures
Digital image correlation to map strain localization and correlate with microstructural changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental observations do not show a statistically significant increase in deformation twinning (e.g., twin density) in the low temperature/high strain-rate regime relative to the high temperature/low strain-rate regime, or if the mechanical responses (such as work hardening or yield stress) do not exhibit the predicted transition between twin-dominated and dislocation-dominated behavior relative to the baseline Co-containing alloys, then the hypothesis will be rejected.
